b: A hashed email, often shortened to HEM, is an email address that has been passed through a cryptographic hash function, most often SHA-256 and occasionally the older MD5, to produce a fixed-length string of letters and numbers. The same address always produces the same string, but the string cannot be turned back into the address by running the function in reverse. That pairing of consistency and one-way output is why the format exists. Two companies holding the same customer can compare hashes and discover the overlap without either sending the readable address. Hashed emails underpin customer list uploads, server-side conversion tracking and login-based identity systems.
How a hashed email is made

The process has three steps, and the first matters more than it looks. Normalisation turns every version of an address into one canonical form. A hash function treats "Jane.Doe@Example.com " and "janedoe@example.com" as entirely different inputs, so a single capital letter or trailing space produces an unrelated output and a failed match. Google's Customer Match and Data Manager API documentation requires whitespace to be trimmed and the address lowercased, and, for gmail.com addresses only, removes periods and anything after a plus sign in the part before the @ symbol. The Unified ID 2.0 (UID2) documentation sets out the same rules.

The second step is hashing. SHA-256, a member of the Secure Hash Algorithm 2 family published by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology in 2001, outputs 256 bits, usually written as a 64-character hexadecimal string. MD5 produces 128 bits, written as 32 characters. UID2 encodes the output in Base64 instead, giving 44 characters, and both sides must agree on encoding.

The third step is comparison. The receiving platform hashes the addresses tied to its own accounts in the same way and looks for identical strings. Matched records join an audience, receive credit for a conversion, or are linked to an identifier. The share that matches is reported as the match rate.

On the buy side, the largest use is list onboarding. An advertiser exports a file from its customer relationship management (CRM) system, hashes the email column and uploads it to Google Customer Match, Meta Custom Audiences, Amazon, Microsoft Advertising, TikTok or, since 2026, ChatGPT ads. Each platform matches the file against its own signed-in users and builds a targeting or exclusion list.

The second use is conversion tracking. When a customer completes a purchase, the advertiser can attach a hashed email to the conversion event so that the platform can tie it to an ad exposure even when cookies are missing. Meta's Conversions API marks email as "hashing required" in its user_data object under the key em. Google's equivalent is enhanced conversions. The IAB Tech Lab's ECAPI 1.0, finalised in May 2026, sets common normalise-then-hash rules for server-to-server conversion APIs across vendors.

On the sell side, publishers collect emails at login or newsletter sign-up and pass hashes to identity providers. UID2, LiveRamp's RampID and the ID5 ID all accept hashed emails as an input. In these systems the hash is a raw material, not the final identifier. UID2, for example, adds a secret salt and hashes again, then encrypts the result into a token that rotates, so that the value travelling in the bid stream is not the HEM itself. The resulting universal IDs are carried in the eids array of OpenRTB 2.6 bid requests, which tells demand-side platforms (DSPs) which provider produced each identifier.

Hash-based matching became standard in advertising when platforms opened their logged-in audiences to advertiser data. Facebook launched Custom Audiences in September 2012, accepting customer files whose emails and phone numbers were hashed before upload. Google followed with Customer Match on September 28, 2015, initially for email addresses only and with a 1,000-address minimum.

The privacy case for hashing was questioned almost from the start. In 2012 Ed Felten, then Chief Technologist at the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC), published a post asking whether hashing made data anonymous and concluded that it did not. On April 9, 2018, Gunes Acar, Steven Englehardt and Arvind Narayanan of Princeton University's Center for Information Technology Policy showed how cheaply hashes could be reversed. They found Datafinder offering to reverse hashed emails for $0.04 each and claiming a 70% recovery rate. One cloud GPU instance, they calculated, could compute 450 billion MD5 hashes per second. "If reversing email hashes were really impossible as claimed, it would cost more than 4 cents," the authors wrote.

The format's commercial weight rose anyway. Apple's App Tracking Transparency, enforced from iOS 14.5 in April 2021, reduced access to the mobile advertising ID. Google's January 2020 plan to phase out third-party cookies in Chrome drove a wave of email-based identity products. The Trade Desk began signing partners for UID2 in October 2020, and LiveRamp renamed IdentityLink as RampID in May 2021.

For advertisers, a hashed email is the most reliable key for carrying first-party data into another company's system. It is a deterministic signal: it matches or it does not, without the guesswork of probabilistic links based on IP address or device characteristics. Retargeting, exclusions, offline sales measurement and conversion modelling all depend on how many hashed records a platform recognises.

For publishers, hashed emails collected at login have become a way to lift prices on inventory that would otherwise carry no identifier. That helps explain the spread of registration walls and newsletter prompts.

The central dispute concerns anonymity. An unsalted SHA-256 hash of a common email address can be recomputed by anyone who already holds the address, which is precisely how platform matching works. On July 24, 2024, staff in the FTC's Office of Technology wrote that "hashes aren't 'anonymous' and can still be used to identify users," and PPC Land reported the warning that claims of anonymity for hashed data may be deceptive. The post cited the FTC's 2022 case against BetterHelp, whose complaint said Facebook could "undo the hashing and reveal the email addresses" shared with it. In Europe, a hashed email is generally treated as pseudonymised rather than anonymised data, which keeps it within the scope of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The Princeton researchers went further, arguing that an unkeyed hash does not even meet the GDPR's definition of pseudonymisation, because no separately held key is involved.

Salting would make reversal harder, but a salt has to be shared for two parties to match, which defeats much of the point. Acar noted that salting "cannot be used when matching email hashes across platforms, devices or vendors."

Vendors disagree about how useful raw hashes are. LiveRamp, in a September 11, 2026 blog post, said hashed emails "are reversible" and claimed its RampID delivered 44% higher match rates than HEM-to-HEM matching; that figure is LiveRamp's own and has not been independently audited.

Coverage is a further limit. Hashed emails exist only for people who log in or subscribe, a minority of visitors on most open-web sites. People also use several addresses, so one customer can appear as two unmatched records.

Encrypted email. Encryption is reversible by anyone holding the key; hashing is designed not to be. Google's shift from requiring SHA-256 hashes to accepting encrypted customer data in Data Manager turns on this difference, since encrypted data can be decrypted and normalised inside a secure environment before matching.

Universal ID. UID2, RampID or ID5 IDs are derived from hashed emails but are separate values: salted, re-hashed, sometimes encrypted and rotated. Passing a universal ID is not the same as passing a HEM.
Salted hash. A salted hash mixes a secret value into the input before hashing. It resists lookup tables but only matches between parties that share the salt.
Anonymous data. Anonymised data cannot be linked back to a person by any reasonably likely means. Regulators on both sides of the Atlantic say a plain hashed email does not meet that bar.

The hashed email has come under pressure from two directions in the autumn of 2026. On October 19, 2026, Apple's WebKit team published "Blocking Identity Resolution Infrastructure," confirming that Safari on iOS, iPadOS, macOS and visionOS 27 blocks network access to third parties that turn email addresses into persistent tracking IDs. The post, signed by John Wilander, Charlie Wolfe and Matthew Finkel, said that "for the majority of users, their email address serves as a globally unique ID that they keep for years, even decades." It named no companies. A WebKit bug filed by The Trade Desk on September 21, 2026 listed domains used by UID2, ID5, LiveRamp and Permutive. Mathieu Roche, chief executive of ID5, called the change "an attack against the business model of the web" and said regulators should examine Apple's practices.

Google, meanwhile, has moved away from the hash itself. An email sent to advertisers and posted on October 18, 2026 said that from November 16, 2026, Google Ads Data Manager would no longer require SHA-256 hashed customer data and would accept encrypted data by default, decrypting, normalising and matching it inside a hardware-isolated trusted execution environment. Google said the change was made for "better performance" and gave no match-rate figure. The move builds on Confidential Matching, the default for Customer Match since September 2024. The plain hash nonetheless remains the default input for most platforms that accept customer lists.

Who: Advertisers, publishers, identity providers such as The Trade Desk (UID2), LiveRamp and ID5, and platforms including Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, TikTok and OpenAI create and match hashed emails. Regulators, including the FTC and European data protection authorities, and browser makers such as Apple set the limits.

What: A hashed email is an email address normalised and passed through a one-way function, usually SHA-256, to produce a fixed string that two parties can compare to find shared customers without exchanging the readable address.

When: Hash-based matching became standard in advertising with Facebook Custom Audiences in 2012 and Google Customer Match in 2015, grew after cookie and mobile ID restrictions from 2020 and 2021, and faced Safari blocks and Google's shift to encrypted matching in October and November 2026.
Where: Hashed emails move through customer list uploads, conversion APIs, clean rooms and identity provider systems whose outputs travel in OpenRTB bid requests, across web, app and connected TV.

Why: Hashing lets companies match first-party data while limiting exposure of raw addresses, but because the same address always yields the same hash, regulators treat it as personal data rather than anonymous data.
